title: Inter-VLAN Routing: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Each floor of the building keeps to itself, and that's on purpose. So how does Sales send a file to Engineering? It needs an elevator.

scenes.heading: Floors and elevators
scenes.narration: Each floor is a V L A N, and people move freely inside it. To go between floors, you need a router, which is the elevator. A router on a stick is one elevator with a single door onto the shared stairwell. It works, but a crowd queues up. A Layer three switch is a whole bank of fast elevators. Each floor's button is a virtual interface called an S V I.

scenes.heading: Two ways to route
scenes.narration: Here's how the two approaches compare. Router on a stick uses one cable, split into sub interfaces. A Layer three switch uses S V Is and routes at wire speed. Pick the switch when speed matters.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three common slip-ups. The switch port facing the router must be a trunk for router on a stick. A Layer three switch won't route until you turn on I P routing. And an S V I stays down unless a port in that V L A N is up.

items.wrong: Any switch port will do for the router
SVIs route out of the box

items.right: Only if a port in that VLAN is up

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva inter-VLAN routing lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Every V L A N needs a gateway, and that's a router or a Layer three switch. Router on a stick means sub interfaces on a trunk. Layer three switches use S V Is, and need I P routing turned on. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva inter-VLAN routing lab.

points.t: Each VLAN needs a router as its gateway
Router on a stick = subinterfaces on a trunk
